nodes.name: $\knf(R)$, the fiber of the cyclotomic trace
nodes.statement: For a ring $R$, we write $\knf(R)$ for the homotopy fiber of the cyclotomic trace $K(R) \to \TC(R)$.
differentia: of the cyclotomic trace $K(R) \to \TC(R)$

nodes.name: Dundas--Goodwillie--McCarthy theorem
nodes.statement: Let $R \to R'$ be a map of rings which is a surjection with nilpotent kernel.\footnote{Or, more generally, a map of connective $\bb{E}_1$-ring spectra such that $\pi_0R\rightarrow\pi_0R'$ is a surjection with nilpotent kernel} Then the map $\knf(R) \to \knf(R')$ is an equivalence.
nodes.statement_short: $\knf$ is invariant under surjections with nilpotent kernel (nil-invariance).
assumptions: Let $R \to R'$ be a map of rings which is a surjection with nilpotent kernel.
conclusions: Then the map $\knf(R) \to \knf(R')$ is an equivalence.

nodes.name: henselian pair
nodes.statement: Let $R$ be a commutative ring and $I \subset R$ an ideal. Then $(R, I)$ is said to be a \emph{henselian pair} if given a polynomial $f(x) \in R[x]$ and a root $\overline{\alpha} \in R/I$ of $\overline{f} \in (R/I)[x]$ with $\overline{f}'(\alpha)$ being a unit of $R/I$, then $\overline \alpha$ lifts to a root $\alpha \in R$ of $f$. Examples of henselian pairs include pairs $(R, I)$ where $R$ is $I$-adically complete (by Hensel's lemma) and pairs $(R, I)$ where $I$ is locally nilpotent.
nodes.origin_citation: classical commutative algebra; cf. Gabber; Stacks Project Tag 09XD
nodes.statement_short: A pair $(R,I)$ is henselian when simple roots mod $I$ always lift to $R$.
nodes.genus: commutative ring $R$ and $I \subset R$ an ideal
differentia: given a polynomial $f(x) \in R[x]$ and a root $\overline{\alpha} \in R/I$ of $\overline{f} \in (R/I)[x]$ with $\overline{f}'(\alpha)$ being a unit of $R/I$, then $\overline \alpha$ lifts to a root $\alpha \in R$ of $f$

nodes.name: Gabber rigidity theorem
nodes.statement: Let $(R, I)$ be a henselian pair. Suppose $n$ is invertible in $R$. Then the map $K(R)/n \to K(R/I)/n$ is an equivalence of spectra.
nodes.statement_short: Mod-$n$ $K$-theory is rigid along a henselian pair when $n$ is invertible.
assumptions: Let $(R, I)$ be a henselian pair.
Suppose $n$ is invertible in $R$.
conclusions: Then the map $K(R)/n \to K(R/I)/n$ is an equivalence of spectra.

nodes.name: Theorem A (main rigidity theorem, introduction form)
nodes.statement: Let $(R, I)$ be a henselian pair. Then for any $n$, the map $\knf(R)/n \to \knf(R/I)/n$ is an equivalence.
nodes.statement_short: $\knf$ with finite coefficients is rigid along any henselian pair.
assumptions: Let $(R, I)$ be a henselian pair.
for any $n$
conclusions: the map $\knf(R)/n \to \knf(R/I)/n$ is an equivalence

nodes.name: Theorem B (Asymptotic comparison of $K, \TC$)
nodes.statement: Let $R$ be a ring henselian along $(p)$ and such that $R/p$ has finite Krull dimension. Let $d = \sup_{x \in \spec (R/p) } \log_p [k(x): k(x)^p]$ where $k(x)$ denotes the residue field at $x$ and $k(x)^p \subset k(x)$ the subfield of $p^\sub{th}$ powers. Then the map $K(R)/p^i \to \TC(R)/p^i$ is a equivalence in degrees $\geq \max(d, 1)$ for each $i \geq 1$.
nodes.statement_short: $p$-adic $K$-theory and $\TC$ agree above degree $d$ for rings henselian along $(p)$.
assumptions: Let $R$ be a ring henselian along $(p)$ and such that $R/p$ has finite Krull dimension.
Let $d = \sup_{x \in \spec (R/p) } \log_p [k(x): k(x)^p]$ where $k(x)$ denotes the residue field at $x$ and $k(x)^p \subset k(x)$ the subfield of $p^\sub{th}$ powers.
conclusions: the map $K(R)/p^i \to \TC(R)/p^i$ is a equivalence in degrees $\geq \max(d, 1)$ for each $i \geq 1$

nodes.name: Theorem C (\'Etale $K$-theory is $\TC$ at points of characteristic $p$)
nodes.statement: Let $R$ be a strictly henselian local ring with residue field of characteristic $p > 0$. Then $\knf(R)/p = 0$, i.e., the map $K(R) \to \TC(R)$ is a $p$-adic equivalence.
nodes.statement_short: On strictly henselian local rings of residue characteristic $p$, the cyclotomic trace is a $p$-adic equivalence.
assumptions: Let $R$ be a strictly henselian local ring with residue field of characteristic $p > 0$.
conclusions: Then $\knf(R)/p = 0$, i.e., the map $K(R) \to \TC(R)$ is a $p$-adic equivalence.

nodes.name: Theorem D (Split injectivity of the cyclotomic trace)
nodes.statement: For any local $\mathbb{F}_p$-algebra $R$ and any $i \geq 1$, the cyclotomic trace $K(R)/p^i \to \TC(R)/p^i$ is split injective on homotopy groups.
nodes.statement_short: The mod $p^i$ cyclotomic trace splits on homotopy for local $\mathbb{F}_p$-algebras.
assumptions: For any local $\mathbb{F}_p$-algebra $R$ and any $i \geq 1$
conclusions: the cyclotomic trace $K(R)/p^i \to \TC(R)/p^i$ is split injective on homotopy groups

nodes.name: Geisser--Levine theorem
nodes.statement: The mod $p$ $K$-groups $K_i(R; \mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}) = \pi_i( K(R)/p)$ are identified with the logarithmic forms $\Omega^{i}_{R, \mathrm{log}}$ for $i \geq 0$.
nodes.statement_short: Mod $p$ $K$-groups of a regular local $\mathbb{F}_p$-algebra are the logarithmic forms.
assumptions: Let $R$ be a local $\mathbb{F}_p$-algebra.
If $R$ is regular
conclusions: The mod $p$ $K$-groups $K_i(R; \mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}) = \pi_i( K(R)/p)$ are identified with the logarithmic forms $\Omega^{i}_{R, \mathrm{log}}$ for $i \geq 0$.

nodes.name: Theorem E (Pro Geisser--Levine, introduction form)
nodes.statement: For any regular local $F$-finite $\mathbb{F}_p$-algebra $R$ and ideal $I \subset R$, there is an isomorphism of pro abelian groups $\{K_i(R/I^n; \mathbb{Z}/p \mathbb{Z})\}_{n \geq 1} \simeq \left\{\Omega^i_{R/I^n, \mathrm{log}}\right\}_{n \geq 1}$ for each $i \geq 0$.
nodes.statement_short: Pro version of Geisser--Levine for the tower $\{R/I^n\}$.
assumptions: For any regular local $F$-finite $\mathbb{F}_p$-algebra $R$ and ideal $I \subset R$
conclusions: there is an isomorphism of pro abelian groups $\{K_i(R/I^n; \mathbb{Z}/p \mathbb{Z})\}_{n \geq 1} \simeq \left\{\Omega^i_{R/I^n, \mathrm{log}}\right\}_{n \geq 1}$ for each $i \geq 0$

nodes.name: Theorem F (Continuity criterion for $K$-theory)
nodes.statement: Let $R$ be a noetherian ring and $I \subset R$ an ideal. Suppose $R$ is $I$-adically complete and $R/p$ is $F$-finite. Then the map $K(R) \to \varprojlim K(R/I^n)$ is a $p$-adic equivalence.
nodes.statement_short: $K$-theory is continuous for complete noetherian rings that are $F$-finite mod $p$.
assumptions: Let $R$ be a noetherian ring and $I \subset R$ an ideal.
Suppose $R$ is $I$-adically complete and $R/p$ is $F$-finite.
conclusions: Then the map $K(R) \to \varprojlim K(R/I^n)$ is a $p$-adic equivalence.

nodes.name: Theorem G ($\TC/p$ is finitary)
nodes.statement: The construction $R \mapsto \TC(R)/p$, from rings $R$ to spectra, commutes with filtered colimits.
nodes.statement_short: $\TC(-)/p$ on rings is a finitary invariant.
conclusions: The construction $R \mapsto \TC(R)/p$, from rings $R$ to spectra, commutes with filtered colimits.

nodes.name: cyclotomic spectrum (Nikolaus--Scholze)
nodes.statement: A {\em cyclotomic spectrum} is a tuple $$ (X , \, \{\varphi_{X, p}: X \to X^{tC_p}\}_{p = 2, 3, 5, \dots }),$$ where $X \in \fun(BS^1, \Sp)$ is a spectrum with an $S^1$-action which is moreover equipped with a map $\varphi_p:X\to X^{tC_p}$ (the {\em cyclotomic Frobenius} at $p$), for each prime number $p$, which is required to be equivariant with respect to the $S^1$-action on $X$ and the $S^1\simeq S^1/C_p$-action on the Tate construction $X^{tC_p}$. By a standard abuse of notation we will occasionally denote a cyclotomic spectrum simply by the underlying spectrum $X$. For the precise definition of the $\infty$-category $\CycSp$ of cyclotomic spectra (whose objects are as above) as a lax equalizer, we refer the reader to \cite[II.1]{nikolaus-scholze}. See \cite[IV.2]{nikolaus-scholze} for a treatment of the symmetric monoidal structure.
nodes.statement_short: A spectrum with $S^1$-action together with equivariant cyclotomic Frobenius maps $\varphi_{X,p}: X \to X^{tC_p}$ for every prime.
differentia: equipped with a map $\varphi_p:X\to X^{tC_p}$ (the {\em cyclotomic Frobenius} at $p$), for each prime number $p$
required to be equivariant with respect to the $S^1$-action on $X$ and the $S^1\simeq S^1/C_p$-action on the Tate construction $X^{tC_p}$

nodes.name: topological cyclic homology $\TC(X)$, $\TC^-$, $\TP$
nodes.statement: Given $X \in \CycSp$, its \emph{topological cyclic homology} $\TC(X) $ is defined as the mapping spectrum $\TC(X) = \hom_{\CycSp}(\mathbf{1}, X)$, where $\mathbf{1} \in \CycSp$ is the unit (cf.~Definition \ref{cons_trivial}). We moreover write \[ \TC^-(X) = X^{hS^1}, \quad \TP(X) = X^{tS^1}\] for its {\em negative topological cyclic homology} and \emph{periodic topological cyclic homology}, the latter having been particularly studied by Hesselholt \cite{hesselholt-tp}.
nodes.statement_short: $\TC(X)$ is mapping spectrum out of the cyclotomic unit; $\TC^-$ and $\TP$ are the $S^1$-homotopy fixed points and Tate construction.
differentia: $\TC(X) = \hom_{\CycSp}(\mathbf{1}, X)$, where $\mathbf{1} \in \CycSp$ is the unit

nodes.name: $\Sp_{\geq n}$ and $\CycSp_{\geq n}$
nodes.statement: Given $n \in \mathbb{Z}$, let $\Sp_{\geq n}$ denote the full subcategory of $\Sp$ consisting of those spectra $X$ that satisfy $\pi_i(X) = 0$ for $i < n$. Let $\CycSp_{\geq n}$ denote the full subcategory of $\CycSp$ consisting of those cyclotomic spectra $(X, \{\varphi_{X,p}\}_{p = 2, 3, 5, \dots} )$ such that the underlying spectrum $X$ belongs to $\Sp_{\geq n}$.
differentia: consisting of those cyclotomic spectra $(X, \{\varphi_{X,p}\}_{p = 2, 3, 5, \dots} )$ such that the underlying spectrum $X$ belongs to $\Sp_{\geq n}$

nodes.name: Fundamental formula for $\TC$ as an equalizer
nodes.statement: \begin{equation} \TC(X) = \mathrm{fib}( \TC^-(X) \xrightarrow{\can_X - \varphi_X} \TP(X)),\end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: $\TC$ is the fiber of $\can_X - \varphi_X: \TC^- \to \TP$.

nodes.name: Classical formula for $\TC$ via $\TR$
nodes.statement: \begin{equation} \TC(X)=\mathrm{fib}(\TR(X;p)\xrightarrow{\mathrm{id}-F}\TR(X;p)).\end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Classical definition of $\TC$ as the fiber of $\mathrm{id}-F$ on $\TR$.

nodes.name: Isotropy separation / fundamental cofiber sequence for $\TR$
nodes.statement: \begin{equation} X_{hC_{p^r}} \to \TR^{r+1}(X;p) \stackrel{R}{\to} \TR^r(X;p) \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Cofiber sequence relating $\TR^{r+1}$, $\TR^r$ and homotopy orbits.

nodes.name: $\THH(R)$ as a cyclotomic spectrum
nodes.statement: A key source of examples of cyclotomic spectra arises as follows. If $R$ is a ring (or, more generally, a structured ring spectrum), then one can form its topological Hochschild homology $\THH(R)$ as an object of $\CycSp$, following \cite[\S III.2]{nikolaus-scholze}. As usual, we will write $\TC(R), \TC^-(R), \TP(R)$ in place of $\TC(\THH(R)), \TC^-(\THH(R)), \TP(\THH(R))$.

nodes.name: Connectivity of $\TC$
nodes.statement: Suppose $X \in \CycSp_{\geq n}$ is $p$-complete. Then $\TC(X) \in \Sp_{\geq n-1}$.
assumptions: Suppose $X \in \CycSp_{\geq n}$ is $p$-complete.
conclusions: Then $\TC(X) \in \Sp_{\geq n-1}$.

nodes.name: Proof of the connectivity lemma
nodes.statement: Using formula (\ref{keyformulaclassical}), it suffices to show that $\TR(X;p) \in \Sp_{\geq n}$; using the Milnor sequence, it is therefore enough to prove that $\TR^r(X;p) \in \Sp_{\geq n}$ and that the Restriction maps $R:\pi_n\TR^{r+1}(X;p) \to \pi_n\TR^{r}(X;p)$ are surjective for all $r\ge1$. But this inductively follows from the basic cofiber sequence (cf.~\cite[Th.~1.2]{Hesselholt}) \begin{equation} X_{hC_{p^r}} \to \TR^{r+1}(X;p) \stackrel{R}{\to} \TR^r(X;p) \end{equation} and the observation that $X_{hC_{p^r}}\in \Sp_{\geq n}$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce via the classical $\TC$ formula and Milnor sequence to connectivity of $\TR^r$, then induct on the isotropy-separation cofiber sequence.

nodes.name: $\TC/p$ commutes with geometric realizations
nodes.statement: The functor $ \TC/p:\CycSp_{\geq 0} \to \Sp$, $X \mapsto \TC(X)/p$ commutes with geometric realizations.
assumptions: The functor $ \TC/p:\CycSp_{\geq 0} \to \Sp$, $X \mapsto \TC(X)/p$
conclusions: commutes with geometric realizations

nodes.name: Proof that $\TC/p$ commutes with geometric realizations
nodes.statement: A geometric realization of connective spectra agrees with its $n^{th}$ partial geometric realization in degrees $<n$. Since $X \mapsto \TC(X)/p=\TC(X/p)$ decreases connectivity at most by one by Lemma \ref{connectivity}, to show that $\TC/p$ commutes with geometric realizations it therefore suffices to show that it commutes with $n^{th}$ partial geometric realizations for all $n$. But these are finite colimits, and are thus preserved by $\TC/p$ since the latter is an exact functor.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to $n$-th partial realizations using the connectivity lemma, then use exactness of $\TC/p$.

nodes.name: $\TC/p$ commutes with all colimits on $\CycSp_{\geq 0}$
nodes.statement: The functor $\TC/p: \CycSp_{\geq 0} \to \Sp$, commutes with all colimits.
nodes.statement_short: Cocontinuity of $\TC/p$ on connective cyclotomic spectra.
assumptions: The functor $\TC/p: \CycSp_{\geq 0} \to \Sp$
conclusions: commutes with all colimits

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem: $\TC/p$ commutes with all colimits
nodes.statement: Consider an $X \in \CycSp_{\geq 0}$ which is $p$-complete. Since $\TC(X\otimes (-)^{\mathrm{triv}})$ is an exact functor from spectra to spectra with value $\TC(X)$ on $S^0$, we get a natural transformation \[ \TC(X) \otimes (-) \to \TC(X \otimes (-)^{\mathrm{triv}}),\] uniquely characterized by being an equivalence on $S^0$, hence on any finite spectrum.\footnote{This is a standard ``assembly map". To construct it rigorously, note that left Kan extension of the restriction of the right hand side to finite spectra is uniquely characterized by its value on $S^0$, by the universal property of spectra among presentable stable $\infty$-categories, and therefore identifies with the left hand side.} By Corollary~\ref{geometricreal}, it is also an equivalence on any geometric realization of finite connective spectra, i.e., for any connective spectrum whose homology groups are finitely generated, e.g., $H \bb F_p$. So we have shown that, for any $X \in \CycSp_{\geq 0}$ which is $p$-complete, there is a natural equivalence $$\TC(X) \otimes H\mathbb{F}_p \simeq \TC(X \otimes H\mathbb{F}_p^{\mathrm{triv}}).$$ Replacing $X$ with $X/p$, the same conclusion follows for an arbitrary $X \in \CycSp_{\geq 0}$. Then from Corollary~\ref{Fpcommutecolimit} we deduce that the functor $X \mapsto \TC(X) \otimes H\mathbb{F}_p$ commutes with colimits in $\CycSp_{\geq 0}$. Hence, given a diagram $I\to\CycSp_{\geq 0}$, the induced map of spectra \begin{equation} \varinjlim_I \TC(X_i) \to \TC(X) \end{equation} becomes an equivalence after smashing with $H\mathbb{F}_p$. Since both sides are bounded below mod $p$ by Lemma \ref{connectivity}, it follows that \eqref{TCcolim} is an equivalence after smashing with $S^0/p$.
nodes.statement_short: Build an assembly map, identify $\TC(X)\otimes H\mathbb{F}_p$ with $\TC(X\otimes H\mathbb{F}_p^{\mathrm{triv}})$, then transfer cocontinuity from $H\mathbb{F}_p^{\mathrm{triv}}$-modules.

nodes.name: Construct the assembly map and identify $\TC \otimes H\mathbb{F}_p$
nodes.statement: Consider an $X \in \CycSp_{\geq 0}$ which is $p$-complete. Since $\TC(X\otimes (-)^{\mathrm{triv}})$ is an exact functor from spectra to spectra with value $\TC(X)$ on $S^0$, we get a natural transformation \[ \TC(X) \otimes (-) \to \TC(X \otimes (-)^{\mathrm{triv}}),\] uniquely characterized by being an equivalence on $S^0$, hence on any finite spectrum.\footnote{This is a standard ``assembly map". To construct it rigorously, note that left Kan extension of the restriction of the right hand side to finite spectra is uniquely characterized by its value on $S^0$, by the universal property of spectra among presentable stable $\infty$-categories, and therefore identifies with the left hand side.} By Corollary~\ref{geometricreal}, it is also an equivalence on any geometric realization of finite connective spectra, i.e., for any connective spectrum whose homology groups are finitely generated, e.g., $H \bb F_p$. So we have shown that, for any $X \in \CycSp_{\geq 0}$ which is $p$-complete, there is a natural equivalence $$\TC(X) \otimes H\mathbb{F}_p \simeq \TC(X \otimes H\mathbb{F}_p^{\mathrm{triv}}).$$
nodes.statement_short: Produce the assembly map and show it is an equivalence after smashing with $H\mathbb{F}_p$.

nodes.name: Deduce cocontinuity mod $p$ from the $H\mathbb{F}_p$-module case
nodes.statement: Replacing $X$ with $X/p$, the same conclusion follows for an arbitrary $X \in \CycSp_{\geq 0}$. Then from Corollary~\ref{Fpcommutecolimit} we deduce that the functor $X \mapsto \TC(X) \otimes H\mathbb{F}_p$ commutes with colimits in $\CycSp_{\geq 0}$. Hence, given a diagram $I\to\CycSp_{\geq 0}$, the induced map of spectra \begin{equation} \varinjlim_I \TC(X_i) \to \TC(X) \end{equation} becomes an equivalence after smashing with $H\mathbb{F}_p$. Since both sides are bounded below mod $p$ by Lemma \ref{connectivity}, it follows that \eqref{TCcolim} is an equivalence after smashing with $S^0/p$.
nodes.statement_short: Transfer colimit-preservation from $H\mathbb{F}_p$-modules and conclude mod $p$ using boundedness below.

nodes.name: Inverse limits of towers in $\CycSp_{\geq 0}$
nodes.statement: There is also a dual assertion which is significantly easier. Suppose we have a tower $\dots \to X_3 \to X_2 \to X_1$ in $\CycSp_{\geq 0}$. Then the inverse limit of the tower $\left\{X_i\right\}$ exists in $\CycSp$ (in fact, in $\CycSp_{\geq -1}$) and is preserved by the forgetful functor $\CycSp \to \Sp$. Indeed, we have $(\varprojlim X_i)^{tC_p} \simeq \varprojlim X_i^{tC_p}$ because the $X_i$'s are uniformly bounded-below, and taking $C_p$-homotopy orbits behaves as a finite colimit in any range of degrees. Then we can appeal to the description of $\CycSp$ as a lax equalizer and \cite[Prop. II.1.5]{nikolaus-scholze}. In particular, it follows that if $X = \varprojlim X_i$ on the level of underlying spectra, then $\TC(X) \simeq \varprojlim \TC(X_i)$.
nodes.statement_short: $\TC$ commutes with inverse limits of towers of uniformly bounded-below cyclotomic spectra.

nodes.name: trivial cyclotomic spectrum $X^{\mathrm{triv}}$ and the cyclotomic sphere
nodes.statement: We have a presentably symmetric monoidal $\infty$-category $\CycSp$, so it receives a unique symmetric monoidal, cocontinuous functor \[ \Sp \to \CycSp,\quad X \mapsto X^{\mathrm{triv}} \] whose right adjoint is the functor $\TC: \CycSp \to \Sp$. More explicitly, this functor $X \mapsto X^{\mathrm{triv}}$ can be identified as follows: $X^\sub{triv}$ has underlying spectrum $X$ equipped with the trivial $S^1$-action; there is therefore a resulting $S^1$-equivariant map $X \to X^{hC_p} = F(BC_{p+}, X)$, and the cyclotomic Frobenius at $p$ for $X^\sub{triv}$ is the composition $\varphi_{X,p}:X\to X^{hC_p} \to X^{tC_p}$. (Notation: when $X$ is a $p$-complete spectrum for a particular prime number $p$, we will tend to drop the $p$ from $\varphi_{X,p}$.) Compare the discussion on \cite[p. 126]{nikolaus-scholze}. For example, taking $X$ to be the sphere spectrum $S^0 \in \Sp$ obtains the {\em cyclotomic sphere spectrum}, which is moreover the unit $\mathbf{1} \in \CycSp$.
nodes.statement_short: The trivial cyclotomic structure functor $\Sp \to \CycSp$, left adjoint to $\TC$; its value on $S^0$ is the cyclotomic sphere and unit.
differentia: $X^\sub{triv}$ has underlying spectrum $X$ equipped with the trivial $S^1$-action
the cyclotomic Frobenius at $p$ for $X^\sub{triv}$ is the composition $\varphi_{X,p}:X\to X^{hC_p} \to X^{tC_p}$

nodes.name: The Frobenius on $\TC^-_*(H\mathbb{F}_p^{\mathrm{triv}})$ annihilates $x$
nodes.statement: The Frobenius map $\varphi_{H \mathbb{F}_p}:\TC^-_*( H \mathbb{F}_p^{\mathrm{triv}}) \to \TP_*(H \mathbb{F}_p^{\mathrm{triv}})$ annihilates $x$.
assumptions: The Frobenius map $\varphi_{H \mathbb{F}_p}:\TC^-_*( H \mathbb{F}_p^{\mathrm{triv}}) \to \TP_*(H \mathbb{F}_p^{\mathrm{triv}})$
conclusions: annihilates $x$

nodes.name: Proof that the Frobenius kills $x$
nodes.statement: There is a commutative diagram of spectra \[ \xymatrix{ \TC^-(H \mathbb{F}_p^{\mathrm{triv}}) \ar[r]^-{\varphi_{H \mathbb{F}_p}} \ar[d]& \TP(H \mathbb{F}_p^{\mathrm{triv}}) \ar[d] \\ H\mathbb{F}_p \ar[r]_{\varphi_{H \bb F_p}} & H \mathbb{F}_p^{tC_p} }\] where the top row is obtained by taking $S^1$-homotopy fixed points on the bottom row via the Tate orbit lemma, \cite[Lem.~II.4.2]{nikolaus-scholze}. The right vertical map $\TP(H\bb F_p^\sub{triv})\to H\mathbb{F}_p^{tC_p}$ is an isomorphism in degree $-2$: indeed, the degree $-2$ generator is invertible in the source by the above calculation of $\TP(H \bb F_p^\sub{triv})$, and therefore necessarily maps to a generator of $\pi_{-2}(H\mathbb{F}_p^{tC_p})$ by multiplicativity. Going both ways around the diagram and noting that of course $\pi_{-2}(H\bb F_p)=0$, we find that $\varphi_{H \mathbb{F}_p}$ must be zero on $\pi_{-2}( \TC^-(H \mathbb{F}_p^{\mathrm{triv}}))$.
nodes.statement_short: Chase a commutative square obtained from the Tate orbit lemma and use $\pi_{-2}(H\mathbb{F}_p)=0$.

nodes.name: Cofiber sequences for $H\mathbb{Z}$-modules with $S^1$-action
nodes.statement: Let $X \in \md_{H \mathbb{Z}}(\Sp^{BS^1})$ be an $H \mathbb{Z}$-module spectrum equipped with an $S^1$-action. Then: \begin{enumerate} \item There is a functorial cofiber sequence of $H\mathbb{Z}$-module spectra \[ \Sigma^{-2} X^{hS^1} \stackrel{x}{\To} X^{hS^1} \To X, \] where the first map is given by multiplication by the generator $x \in \pi_{-2}(H \mathbb{Z}^{hS^1}) = H^2( \mathbb{CP}^\infty; \mathbb{Z})$. \item There is a functorial cofiber sequence of $H \mathbb{Z}$-modules \[ X \to X_{hS^1} \to \Sigma^2 X_{hS^1} . \] \item There is moreover a functorial cofiber sequence \[ \Sigma^{-2} X^{hS^1} \xto{x \mathrm{can}_X} X^{tS^1} \To X_{hS^1}, \] where $\mathrm{can}_X: X^{hS^1} \to X^{tS^1}$ is the canonical map. \end{enumerate}
nodes.origin_citation: Nikolaus--Scholze, Lemma IV.4.12; cf. Loday Sec. 2.2
nodes.statement_short: Three functorial cofiber sequences relating $X$, $X^{hS^1}$, $X_{hS^1}$, $X^{tS^1}$ and multiplication by $x$.
assumptions: Let $X \in \md_{H \mathbb{Z}}(\Sp^{BS^1})$ be an $H \mathbb{Z}$-module spectrum equipped with an $S^1$-action.
conclusions: There is a functorial cofiber sequence of $H\mathbb{Z}$-module spectra \[ \Sigma^{-2} X^{hS^1} \stackrel{x}{\To} X^{hS^1} \To X, \]
There is a functorial cofiber sequence of $H \mathbb{Z}$-modules \[ X \to X_{hS^1} \to \Sigma^2 X_{hS^1} . \]
There is moreover a functorial cofiber sequence \[ \Sigma^{-2} X^{hS^1} \xto{x \mathrm{can}_X} X^{tS^1} \To X_{hS^1}, \]

nodes.name: Proof of the cofiber-sequence lemma
nodes.statement: Assertion (1) is \cite[Lemma~IV.4.12]{nikolaus-scholze}, in view of the cofiber sequence of $H\mathbb{Z}^{hS^1}$-modules $\Sigma^{-2} H\mathbb{Z}^{hS^1} \xrightarrow{x} H\mathbb{Z}^{hS^1} \to H\mathbb{Z}$. For assertion (2), by \emph{loc.~cit.}, we have functorial equivalences $X^{tS^1} \simeq X^{hS^1} \otimes_{H\mathbb{Z}^{hS^1}} H\mathbb{Z}^{tS^1} = X^{hS^1}[1/x]$. The fiber sequences $\Sigma (H\mathbb{Z})_{hS^1} \to H\mathbb{Z}^{hS^1} \to H\mathbb{Z}^{tS^1}$ and $\Sigma X_{hS^1} \to X^{hS^1} \to X^{tS^1}$ make $(H\mathbb{Z})_{hS^1}$ into an $H\mathbb{Z}^{hS^1} $-module and yield a natural equivalence $X_{hS^1} \simeq X^{hS^1} \otimes_{H\mathbb{Z}^{hS^1}} (H\mathbb{Z})_{hS^1}$. Using the fiber sequence of $H\mathbb{Z}^{hS^1}$-modules $H\mathbb{Z} \to (H\mathbb{Z})_{hS^1} \xrightarrow{x} \Sigma^2 (H \mathbb{Z})_{hS^1}$, we obtain the assertion (2). Assertion (3) follows from assertion (1) and from the cofiber sequence $X^{hS^1} \stackrel{\mathrm{can}_X}{\to} X^{tS^1} \to \Sigma^2 X_{hS^1}$, where we use that multiplication by $x$ is an equivalence on $X^{tS^1}$.
nodes.statement_short: Deduce each assertion from the $x$-multiplication cofiber sequence on $H\mathbb{Z}^{hS^1}$ by base change.

nodes.name: Assertion (1) from Nikolaus--Scholze
nodes.statement: Assertion (1) is \cite[Lemma~IV.4.12]{nikolaus-scholze}, in view of the cofiber sequence of $H\mathbb{Z}^{hS^1}$-modules $\Sigma^{-2} H\mathbb{Z}^{hS^1} \xrightarrow{x} H\mathbb{Z}^{hS^1} \to H\mathbb{Z}$.
nodes.statement_short: Cite the $x$-multiplication cofiber sequence for $H\mathbb{Z}^{hS^1}$.

nodes.name: Assertion (2) by base change along $H\mathbb{Z}^{hS^1}$
nodes.statement: For assertion (2), by \emph{loc.~cit.}, we have functorial equivalences $X^{tS^1} \simeq X^{hS^1} \otimes_{H\mathbb{Z}^{hS^1}} H\mathbb{Z}^{tS^1} = X^{hS^1}[1/x]$. The fiber sequences $\Sigma (H\mathbb{Z})_{hS^1} \to H\mathbb{Z}^{hS^1} \to H\mathbb{Z}^{tS^1}$ and $\Sigma X_{hS^1} \to X^{hS^1} \to X^{tS^1}$ make $(H\mathbb{Z})_{hS^1}$ into an $H\mathbb{Z}^{hS^1} $-module and yield a natural equivalence $X_{hS^1} \simeq X^{hS^1} \otimes_{H\mathbb{Z}^{hS^1}} (H\mathbb{Z})_{hS^1}$. Using the fiber sequence of $H\mathbb{Z}^{hS^1}$-modules $H\mathbb{Z} \to (H\mathbb{Z})_{hS^1} \xrightarrow{x} \Sigma^2 (H \mathbb{Z})_{hS^1}$, we obtain the assertion (2).
nodes.statement_short: Identify $X_{hS^1}$ by base change and apply the $x$-sequence for $(H\mathbb{Z})_{hS^1}$.

nodes.name: Assertion (3) from (1) and invertibility of $x$ on $X^{tS^1}$
nodes.statement: Assertion (3) follows from assertion (1) and from the cofiber sequence $X^{hS^1} \stackrel{\mathrm{can}_X}{\to} X^{tS^1} \to \Sigma^2 X_{hS^1}$, where we use that multiplication by $x$ is an equivalence on $X^{tS^1}$.
nodes.statement_short: Combine (1) with the canonical-map cofiber sequence.

nodes.name: Functorial fiber sequence $\TC(X) \to X \to X_{hS^1}$
nodes.statement: For $X \in \md_{H \mathbb{F}_p^{\mathrm{triv}}}( \CycSp)$, there exists a functorial fiber sequence \begin{equation} \TC(X) \To X \To X_{hS^1}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: For $H\mathbb{F}_p^{\mathrm{triv}}$-modules, $\TC(X)$ is the fiber of $X \to X_{hS^1}$.
assumptions: For $X \in \md_{H \mathbb{F}_p^{\mathrm{triv}}}( \CycSp)$
conclusions: there exists a functorial fiber sequence \begin{equation} \TC(X) \To X \To X_{hS^1}. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Proof of the functorial fiber sequence
nodes.statement: We show first that, for $X \in \md_{H \mathbb{F}_p^{\mathrm{triv}}}(\CycSp) $, the composition \begin{equation} \Sigma^{-2} \TC^-(X) \xTo{x} \TC^-(X) \xrightarrow{\varphi_X} \TP(X) \end{equation} is functorially nullhomotopic. In fact, since $X$ is an $H \mathbb{F}_p^{\mathrm{triv}}$-module, we find that $\TC^-(X)$ is an $\TC^-( H \mathbb{F}_p^{\mathrm{triv}})$-module, $\TP(X)$ is a $\TP(H \mathbb{F}_p^{\mathrm{triv}})$-module, and the map $\varphi_X$ is $\varphi_{H \bb F_p}$-linear. We obtain a resulting functorial commutative diagram, where the base-changes are along $\varphi_{ H \bb F_p}: \TC^-(H \mathbb{F}_p^{\mathrm{triv}}) \to \TP( H \mathbb{F}_p^{\mathrm{triv}})$, \begin{equation} \xymatrix@C=1cm{ \Sigma^{-2} \TC^-(X) \ar[r]^x \ar[d] & \TC^-(X) \ar[d] \ar[rd]^{\varphi_X} \\ \Sigma^{-2} \TC^-(X) \otimes_{\TC^-(H \mathbb{F}_p^{\mathrm{triv}})} \TP(H \mathbb{F}_p^{\mathrm{triv}}) \ar[r]_-{\varphi_{H \bb F_p}(x)} & \TC^-(X) \otimes_{\TC^-(H\mathbb{F}_p^{\mathrm{triv}})} \TP(H \mathbb{F}_p^{\mathrm{triv}}) \ar[r] & \TP(X) } .\end{equation} However $\varphi_{H \mathbb{F}_p}(x)$ vanishes, by Lemma~\ref{Frobvanish}, and so the composite \eqref{th} is functorially nullhomotopic as desired. It now follows that there is a functorial commutative diagram \begin{equation} \xymatrix{ \Sigma^{-2} \TC^-(X) \ar[d]_{x} \ar[r]^{\mathrm{id}} &\Sigma^{-2} \TC^-(X)\ar[d]^{x \mathrm{can}_X} \\ \TC^-(X) \ar[r]_{\mathrm{can}_X-\varphi_X} & \TP(X) } \end{equation} in which the fiber of the bottom arrow is $\TC(X)$ by formula \eqref{keyformula}. Therefore $\TC(X)$ is also the fiber of the natural map $X \to X_{hS^1}$ between the cofibers of the vertical arrows in the above diagram, where we identify the cofibers using Lemma~\ref{cofiberofx}.
nodes.statement_short: Show $\varphi_X \circ x$ is nullhomotopic using $\varphi_{H\mathbb{F}_p}(x)=0$, then take cofibers of the vertical maps in the resulting square.

nodes.name: Show the composite $\varphi_X \circ x$ is nullhomotopic
nodes.statement: We show first that, for $X \in \md_{H \mathbb{F}_p^{\mathrm{triv}}}(\CycSp) $, the composition \begin{equation} \Sigma^{-2} \TC^-(X) \xTo{x} \TC^-(X) \xrightarrow{\varphi_X} \TP(X) \end{equation} is functorially nullhomotopic. In fact, since $X$ is an $H \mathbb{F}_p^{\mathrm{triv}}$-module, we find that $\TC^-(X)$ is an $\TC^-( H \mathbb{F}_p^{\mathrm{triv}})$-module, $\TP(X)$ is a $\TP(H \mathbb{F}_p^{\mathrm{triv}})$-module, and the map $\varphi_X$ is $\varphi_{H \bb F_p}$-linear. We obtain a resulting functorial commutative diagram, where the base-changes are along $\varphi_{ H \bb F_p}: \TC^-(H \mathbb{F}_p^{\mathrm{triv}}) \to \TP( H \mathbb{F}_p^{\mathrm{triv}})$, \begin{equation} \xymatrix@C=1cm{ \Sigma^{-2} \TC^-(X) \ar[r]^x \ar[d] & \TC^-(X) \ar[d] \ar[rd]^{\varphi_X} \\ \Sigma^{-2} \TC^-(X) \otimes_{\TC^-(H \mathbb{F}_p^{\mathrm{triv}})} \TP(H \mathbb{F}_p^{\mathrm{triv}}) \ar[r]_-{\varphi_{H \bb F_p}(x)} & \TC^-(X) \otimes_{\TC^-(H\mathbb{F}_p^{\mathrm{triv}})} \TP(H \mathbb{F}_p^{\mathrm{triv}}) \ar[r] & \TP(X) } .\end{equation} However $\varphi_{H \mathbb{F}_p}(x)$ vanishes, by Lemma~\ref{Frobvanish}, and so the composite \eqref{th} is functorially nullhomotopic as desired.
nodes.statement_short: Use $\varphi_{H\mathbb{F}_p}$-linearity plus the vanishing lemma to kill $\varphi_X \circ x$.

nodes.name: Take cofibers to identify $\TC(X)$ as the fiber of $X \to X_{hS^1}$
nodes.statement: It now follows that there is a functorial commutative diagram \begin{equation} \xymatrix{ \Sigma^{-2} \TC^-(X) \ar[d]_{x} \ar[r]^{\mathrm{id}} &\Sigma^{-2} \TC^-(X)\ar[d]^{x \mathrm{can}_X} \\ \TC^-(X) \ar[r]_{\mathrm{can}_X-\varphi_X} & \TP(X) } \end{equation} in which the fiber of the bottom arrow is $\TC(X)$ by formula \eqref{keyformula}. Therefore $\TC(X)$ is also the fiber of the natural map $X \to X_{hS^1}$ between the cofibers of the vertical arrows in the above diagram, where we identify the cofibers using Lemma~\ref{cofiberofx}.
nodes.statement_short: Pass to cofibers of the vertical maps and identify them via the cofiber-sequence lemma.

nodes.name: $\TC$ commutes with colimits on $H\mathbb{F}_p^{\mathrm{triv}}$-modules
nodes.statement: The functor $\md_{H \mathbb{F}_p^{\mathrm{triv}}}(\CycSp) \to \Sp$ given by $X \mapsto \TC(X)$ commutes with all colimits. That is, the unit of the presentably symmetric monoidal stable $\infty$-category $\md_{H \mathbb{F}_p^{\mathrm{triv}}}(\CycSp)$ is compact.
assumptions: The functor $\md_{H \mathbb{F}_p^{\mathrm{triv}}}(\CycSp) \to \Sp$ given by $X \mapsto \TC(X)$
conclusions: commutes with all colimits
the unit of the presentably symmetric monoidal stable $\infty$-category $\md_{H \mathbb{F}_p^{\mathrm{triv}}}(\CycSp)$ is compact

nodes.name: Proof that $\TC$ is cocontinuous on $H\mathbb{F}_p^{\mathrm{triv}}$-modules
nodes.statement: Since passage to homotopy orbits commutes with all colimits, this follows from Proposition \ref{functorialfibseq}.
nodes.statement_short: Immediate from the functorial fiber sequence, since homotopy orbits are cocontinuous.

nodes.name: Alternative proof of the connectivity of $\TC$
nodes.statement: Let $X \in \CycSp_{ \geq 0}$ be $p$-complete. Using the functorial fiber sequence of Proposition~\ref{functorialfibseq}, we can give an independent proof of Lemma~\ref{connectivity} (and thus of Corollary~\ref{geometricreal}) which is independent of the classical approach to $\TC$ (i.e., based entirely on the formula \eqref{keyformula}). Namely, we argue that $\TC(X) \in \Sp_{\geq -1}$. First, suppose that $X$ is an $H \mathbb{F}_p^{\mathrm{triv}}$-module. In this case, we find that $\TC(X) \in \Sp_{\geq -1}$ thanks to Proposition~\ref{functorialfibseq}. More generally, if $X$ is a $p$-complete $H \mathbb{Z}^{\mathrm{triv}}$-module, then we find that $X/p$ is an $H\mathbb{F}_p^{\mathrm{triv}}$-module so that $\TC(X/p) \simeq \TC(X)/p$ belongs to $\Sp_{\geq -1}$; by $p$-completeness we deduce that $\TC(X) \in \Sp_{\geq -1}$. In general, let $X \in \CycSp_{\geq 0}$ be an arbitrary $p$-complete object. Then, we consider the Adams tower for $X$ with respect to the commutative algebra object $H\mathbb{Z}^{\mathrm{triv}} \in \CycSp$, i.e., the tower for the totalization of the cosimplicial object $X \otimes (H\mathbb{Z}^{\mathrm{triv}})^{\otimes \bullet + 1}$ (cf.~\cite[Sec.~2.1]{MNN17} for a reference in this generality). That is, we consider the tower $\left\{X_n\right\} \in \CycSp$ defined inductively such that $X_0 = X$ and $X_{n+1}$ is the fiber of the map $X_{n} \to X_n \otimes H\mathbb{Z}^{\mathrm{triv}}$. One sees easily that $X_n \in \CycSp_{\geq n}$, and that $X_n$ is $p$-complete since $\pi_i(S^0)$ is finite for $i>0$. Since $X_{n}/X_{n+1}$ is a $H\mathbb{Z}^{\mathrm{triv}}$-module, it follows from the previous analysis that $\TC(X_n/X_{n+1}) \in \Sp_{\geq (n-1)}$ for each $n$. Inductively, it follows now that $\TC(X/X_{n+1}) = \TC(X_0/X_{n+1}) \in \Sp_{\geq -1}$ for each $n$ and that the maps $\TC(X/X_{n+1}) \to \TC(X/X_{n})$ are surjective on $\pi_{-1}$. Since $X \to X/X_{n+1}$ is an equivalence in degrees $\leq n$, it follows (as in \cite[Lem.~I.2.6]{nikolaus-scholze}) that \[ X^{hS^1} \simeq \varprojlim (X/X_n )^{hS^1}, \quad X^{tS^1} \simeq \varprojlim (X/X_n)^{tS^1} \] and therefore by \eqref{keyformula} \[ \TC(X) \simeq \varprojlim \TC(X/X_n). \] Using the Milnor exact sequence and the connectivity properties of $\TC(X/X_{n+1})$, one concludes that $\TC(X) \in \Sp_{\geq -1}$.
nodes.statement_short: Reprove $\TC(X) \in \Sp_{\geq -1}$ purely Nikolaus--Scholze-theoretically, via the Adams tower along $H\mathbb{Z}^{\mathrm{triv}}$.

nodes.name: $\TC(-)/p$ on rings commutes with sifted colimits
nodes.statement: The functor $\mathrm{Alg}(\Sp_{\geq 0})\to\Sp$, $R \mapsto \TC(R)/p$ commutes with sifted colimits.
nodes.statement_short: $\TC/p$ of connective ring spectra is finitary and commutes with geometric realizations.
assumptions: The functor $\mathrm{Alg}(\Sp_{\geq 0})\to\Sp$, $R \mapsto \TC(R)/p$
conclusions: commutes with sifted colimits

nodes.name: Proof that $\TC(-)/p$ commutes with sifted colimits
nodes.statement: This follows from Theorem~\ref{TCcommutes} since $\TC(R) = \TC( \THH(R))$, where we note that the topological Hochschild homology functor $\THH: \mathrm{Alg}(\Sp_{\geq 0}) \to \CycSp_{\geq 0}$ commutes with sifted colimits (as geometric realizations and tensor products do).
nodes.statement_short: Compose the cocontinuity of $\TC/p$ with the sifted-cocontinuity of $\THH$.

nodes.name: Deducing the corollary for commutative $\mathbb{F}_p$-algebras via de Rham--Witt
nodes.statement: For commutative $\mathbb{F}_p$-algebras, Corollary~\ref{TCring} can be deduced using the description of Hesselholt \cite{Hesselholt} of $\THH$ of smooth $\mathbb{F}_p$-algebras in terms of the de Rham--Witt complex; we detail this in subsection~\ref{dRWapproach} below.

nodes.name: The $p$-limit axiom in McCarthy's theorem
nodes.statement: In the case of square-zero extensions, the verification (called the \emph{$p$-limit axiom}) of Corollary~\ref{TCring} plays an important role in the proof that relative $K$-theory and $\TC$ with finite coefficients agree for nilimmersions of rings in McCarthy \cite{mccarthy}.

nodes.name: Spherical monoid rings and Frobenius lifts
nodes.statement: Let $M$ be an $\mathbb{E}_1$-monoid in the $\infty$-category of spaces, so that one can form the spherical monoid ring $\Sigma^\infty_+ M$. The formula for $\TC$ of spherical monoid rings \cite[Lemma IV.3.1]{nikolaus-scholze} (preceded by the formula for spherical group rings appearing already in \cite[Eq. (0.3)]{BHM}) shows that for any such $R$, the cyclotomic structure map $\THH(R) \to \THH(R)^{tC_p}$ factors $S^1$-equivariantly through $\THH(R)^{hC_p}$, which is called a \emph{Frobenius lift} in \cite{nikolaus-scholze}. For cyclotomic spectrum $X$ with a Frobenius lift, the construction of ($p$-complete) $\TC$ simplifies: one has a fiber square \cite[Prop. IV-3.4]{nikolaus-scholze} relating $\TC(X)$ to $\Sigma X_{hS^1}$ and two copies of $X$. It follows from this that the construction $M \mapsto \TC( \Sigma^\infty_+ M)/p$ commutes with filtered colimits in $M$. Since the free associative algebra is a spherical monoid ring, and since $\TC$ is already known to commute with geometric realizations, one can also deduce Corollary~\ref{TCring} in this way.
nodes.statement_short: For spherical monoid rings the cyclotomic Frobenius lifts, giving an independent route to the finitariness of $\TC/p$.

nodes.name: Strong finiteness: approximating $\TC/p$ by homotopy-orbit functors
nodes.statement: For any given integer $n$, there exists a functor $F \in \fun_{}(\CycSp_{\geq 0}, \Sp)$ with the following properties: \begin{enumerate} \item $F$ belongs to the thick subcategory of $\fun_{}(\CycSp_{\geq 0}, \Sp)$ generated by the functor $X \mapsto (X\otimes H\mathbb{F}_p^\sub{triv})_{hS^1}$; \item There exists an equivalence $\tau_{\leq n} F(X) \simeq \tau_{\leq n}(\TC(X)/p)$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: In any given range, $\TC/p$ is finitely built from $X \mapsto (X\otimes H\mathbb{F}_p^{\mathrm{triv}})_{hS^1}$.
assumptions: For any given integer $n$
conclusions: there exists a functor $F \in \fun_{}(\CycSp_{\geq 0}, \Sp)$ with the following properties: \begin{enumerate} \item $F$ belongs to the thick subcategory of $\fun_{}(\CycSp_{\geq 0}, \Sp)$ generated by the functor $X \mapsto (X\otimes H\mathbb{F}_p^\sub{triv})_{hS^1}$
There exists an equivalence $\tau_{\leq n} F(X) \simeq \tau_{\leq n}(\TC(X)/p)$.

nodes.name: Proof of the strong finiteness proposition
nodes.statement: We claim that for each $n$, the functor $X \mapsto \TC(X\otimes \tau_{\leq n+1}(S^0/p)^\sub{triv})$ has the desired properties. Indeed, it belongs to the thick subcategory generated by $X \mapsto (X\otimes H\mathbb{F}_p^\sub{triv})_{hS^1}$ thanks to Proposition~\ref{functorialfibseq} and assertion~(\ref{hS1cofib}) of Lemma~\ref{cofiberofx}, while the connectivity assertion follows from Lemma~\ref{connectivity}.
nodes.statement_short: Exhibit $X \mapsto \TC(X\otimes \tau_{\leq n+1}(S^0/p)^{\mathrm{triv}})$ as the required functor.

nodes.name: Pro-vanishing criterion for towers of functors into $\mathrm{Ab}$
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{C}$ be a category admitting countable coproducts, and consider a tower of functors $\mathcal{C}\rightarrow \operatorname{Ab}$, say $\ldots \rightarrow F_r\rightarrow F_{r-1}\rightarrow \ldots \rightarrow F_1$. Suppose that: \begin{enumerate} \item For each $X\in\mathcal{C}$ we have $\varprojlim_r F_r(X) = \varprojlim^1_r F_r(X) = 0$. \item For each $r\in\mathbb{N}$, the functor $F_r$ commutes with countable coproducts. \end{enumerate} Then the tower $\{F_r\}_{r \geq 1}$ is pro-zero, i.e.\ it is zero as an object of $\operatorname{Pro}(\operatorname{Fun}(\mathcal{C},\operatorname{Ab}))$; or, equivalently, for all $r\in\mathbb{N}$ there is an $s>r$ such that the morphism $F_s\rightarrow F_r$ is $0$.
nodes.statement_short: Vanishing of $\varprojlim$ and $\varprojlim^1$ plus coproduct-preservation forces a tower of abelian-group-valued functors to be pro-zero.
assumptions: Let $\mathcal{C}$ be a category admitting countable coproducts, and consider a tower of functors $\mathcal{C}\rightarrow \operatorname{Ab}$, say $\ldots \rightarrow F_r\rightarrow F_{r-1}\rightarrow \ldots \rightarrow F_1$.
For each $X\in\mathcal{C}$ we have $\varprojlim_r F_r(X) = \varprojlim^1_r F_r(X) = 0$.
For each $r\in\mathbb{N}$, the functor $F_r$ commutes with countable coproducts.
conclusions: Then the tower $\{F_r\}_{r \geq 1}$ is pro-zero, i.e.\ it is zero as an object of $\operatorname{Pro}(\operatorname{Fun}(\mathcal{C},\operatorname{Ab}))$

nodes.name: Proof of the pro-vanishing criterion (abelian case)
nodes.statement: First we show the weaker claim that for all $X\in\mathcal{C}$, the tower $\{F_r(X)\}_r$ of abelian groups is pro-zero. Set $M_r = F_r(X)$ for brevity. From the hypothesis we find that an infinite direct sum of copies of the tower $\{M_r\}_r$ has vanishing $\varprojlim^1$; thus \cite[Cor.~6]{Emmanouil} implies that $\{M_r\}_r$ is Mittag--Leffler, i.e., for each $r$, the descending sequence $\{\mathrm{im}(M_s \to M_r)\}_{s \geq r}$ of submodules of $M_r$ stabilizes. If this stable submodule were nonzero for some $r$, we would deduce the existence of a nonzero element of $\varprojlim_s M_s$, contradicting the hypothesis. Thus the stable value is $0$ for all $r$, which exactly means that $\{M_r\}_r$ is pro-zero. Now, suppose the claim of the lemma does not hold, i.e., that $\{F_r\}_r$ is not pro-zero. Then for each $r\in\mathbb{N}$ and $s>r$, we can find an $Y\in\mathcal{C}$ such that $F_s(Y)\rightarrow F_r(Y)$ is nonzero. Let $X$ denote the coproduct over all pairs $s>r$ of a choice of such a $Y$. Then for every $s>r$ the map $F_s(X)\rightarrow F_r(X)$ is nonzero, so we deduce that the tower $\{F_r(X)\}$ is not pro-zero, in contradiction to what was established above.
nodes.statement_short: Pointwise pro-vanishing via Mittag--Leffler, then globalize by a coproduct trick and contradiction.

nodes.name: Pointwise pro-vanishing via Mittag--Leffler
nodes.statement: First we show the weaker claim that for all $X\in\mathcal{C}$, the tower $\{F_r(X)\}_r$ of abelian groups is pro-zero. Set $M_r = F_r(X)$ for brevity. From the hypothesis we find that an infinite direct sum of copies of the tower $\{M_r\}_r$ has vanishing $\varprojlim^1$; thus \cite[Cor.~6]{Emmanouil} implies that $\{M_r\}_r$ is Mittag--Leffler, i.e., for each $r$, the descending sequence $\{\mathrm{im}(M_s \to M_r)\}_{s \geq r}$ of submodules of $M_r$ stabilizes. If this stable submodule were nonzero for some $r$, we would deduce the existence of a nonzero element of $\varprojlim_s M_s$, contradicting the hypothesis. Thus the stable value is $0$ for all $r$, which exactly means that $\{M_r\}_r$ is pro-zero.
nodes.statement_short: Deduce the Mittag--Leffler condition from vanishing $\varprojlim^1$ and conclude pointwise pro-vanishing.

nodes.name: Globalize by taking a coproduct of counterexamples
nodes.statement: Now, suppose the claim of the lemma does not hold, i.e., that $\{F_r\}_r$ is not pro-zero. Then for each $r\in\mathbb{N}$ and $s>r$, we can find an $Y\in\mathcal{C}$ such that $F_s(Y)\rightarrow F_r(Y)$ is nonzero. Let $X$ denote the coproduct over all pairs $s>r$ of a choice of such a $Y$. Then for every $s>r$ the map $F_s(X)\rightarrow F_r(X)$ is nonzero, so we deduce that the tower $\{F_r(X)\}$ is not pro-zero, in contradiction to what was established above.
nodes.statement_short: Assemble a single object from all counterexamples to contradict the pointwise claim.

nodes.name: Pro-vanishing criterion for towers of spectrum-valued functors
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{C}$ be an $\infty$-category admitting countable coproducts, and consider a tower of functors $\mathcal{C}\rightarrow \operatorname{Sp}$, say $\ldots \rightarrow F_r\rightarrow F_{r-1}\ldots \rightarrow F_1$. Suppose that: \begin{enumerate} \item For each $X\in\mathcal{C}$ we have $\varprojlim_r F_r(X) = 0$. \item For each $r\in\mathbb{N}$, the functor $F_r$ commutes with countable coproducts. \item The homotopy groups of each $F_r(X)$ are zero outside some fixed interval $[a,b]$, independent of $X$ and $r$. \end{enumerate} Then the tower $\{F_r\}_{r \geq 1}$ is pro-zero, i.e.\ it is zero as an object of $\operatorname{Pro}(\operatorname{Fun}(\mathcal{C},\operatorname{Sp}))$.
nodes.statement_short: Spectral analog of the pro-vanishing criterion, under a uniform homotopy-group range hypothesis.
assumptions: Let $\mathcal{C}$ be an $\infty$-category admitting countable coproducts, and consider a tower of functors $\mathcal{C}\rightarrow \operatorname{Sp}$, say $\ldots \rightarrow F_r\rightarrow F_{r-1}\ldots \rightarrow F_1$.
For each $X\in\mathcal{C}$ we have $\varprojlim_r F_r(X) = 0$.
For each $r\in\mathbb{N}$, the functor $F_r$ commutes with countable coproducts.
The homotopy groups of each $F_r(X)$ are zero outside some fixed interval $[a,b]$, independent of $X$ and $r$.
conclusions: Then the tower $\{F_r\}_{r \geq 1}$ is pro-zero, i.e.\ it is zero as an object of $\operatorname{Pro}(\operatorname{Fun}(\mathcal{C},\operatorname{Sp}))$.

nodes.name: Proof of the spectral pro-vanishing criterion
nodes.statement: The Milnor sequence and induction up the Postnikov tower show that (1) implies $\varprojlim_r \pi_i F_r(X) = \varprojlim^1_r \pi_i F_r(X) = 0$ for all $i\in\mathbb{Z}$. Since $\pi_i$ commutes with coproducts, we can apply the previous lemma to $\{\pi_i F_r\}_r$ and conclude that each tower $\{\pi_i F_r\}_r$ is pro-zero. Thus each Postnikov section of $\{F_r\}_r$ is pro-zero, and therefore so is $\{F_r\}_r$ itself, by devissage up the (finite) Postnikov tower.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to homotopy groups via the Milnor sequence and apply the abelian pro-vanishing lemma, then d\'evissage.

nodes.name: Pro-constancy of the tower $\{\TC^r(-)/p\}$
nodes.statement: Fix an integer $k$. Then the tower of objects of $\operatorname{Fun}(\CycSp_{\geq 0},\operatorname{Sp})$ given by $ \left\{ \tau_{\leq k}(\TC^r(-)/p)\right\}_{r}$ is pro-constant with value $\tau_{\leq k}(\TC(-)/p)$.
nodes.statement_short: Truncated $\{\TC^r(-)/p\}_r$ is pro-constant with value $\TC(-)/p$; a restatement of the finitariness theorem.
assumptions: Fix an integer $k$.
conclusions: the tower of objects of $\operatorname{Fun}(\CycSp_{\geq 0},\operatorname{Sp})$ given by $ \left\{ \tau_{\leq k}(\TC^r(-)/p)\right\}_{r}$ is pro-constant with value $\tau_{\leq k}(\TC(-)/p)$

nodes.name: Proof of pro-constancy of $\{\TC^r(-)/p\}$
nodes.statement: Setting $F_{r}(X) \stackrel{\mathrm{def}}{=} \tau_{\leq k+1}\mathrm{cofib}( \TC(X)/p \to \TC^r(X)/p)$, we will show that the tower $\{F_{r}(-)\}_r$ is pro-zero. As $k$ varies, this shows that the map $\left\{\TC(-)/p\right\} \to \left\{\TC^r(-)/p\right\}_r$ is a pro-isomorphism on each homotopy group in degrees $\leq k$ (in the pro-category of functors $\CycSp_{\geq 0} \to \mathrm{Ab}$), which is enough to conclude. Certainly $\varprojlim_r F_{r}(X) = 0$, and $F_r$ commutes with arbitrary coproducts by Theorem~\ref{TCcommutes}, so the desired claim follows from Lemma~\ref{invlim02}.
nodes.statement_short: Apply the spectral pro-vanishing lemma to the truncated cofiber functors $F_r$.

nodes.name: inverse Cartier operator $C^{-1}$
nodes.statement: The \emph{inverse Cartier operator} $C^{-1}: \Omega^n_R \to H^n(\Omega^{\ast}_R) \subset \Omega^n_R/d \Omega^{n-1}_R$ is the multiplicative operator uniquely characterized by the formulas \( C^{-1}(a) = a^p, \quad C^{-1}(db) = b^{p-1} db, \) for $a, b \in R$. See \cite{Cartier1957}, also \cite[Prop.~3.3.4]{BLM}, for a construction of this map.
differentia: uniquely characterized by the formulas \( C^{-1}(a) = a^p, \quad C^{-1}(db) = b^{p-1} db, \) for $a, b \in R$

nodes.name: the de Rham--Witt complex $W_r\Omega^{\ast}_R$
nodes.statement: Let $R$ be an $\bb F_p$-algebra. For $r\ge 1$, we denote as usual by \[W_r(R)\xto{d}W_r\Omega^1_R\xto{d}W_r\Omega^2_R\xto{d}\cdots\] the classical de Rham--Witt complex (more precisely, differential graded algebras) of Bloch--Deligne--Illusie \cite{illusie-derham-witt}; this is the usual de Rham complex $\Omega^\bullet_R$ in the case $r=1$. We recall that the individual de Rham--Witt groups are equipped with Restriction and Frobenius maps $R,F:W_r\Omega^n_R\to W_{r-1}\Omega^n_R$. We let $W \Omega_R^{\ast}$ denote the inverse limit of the tower $\left\{W_r \Omega^{\ast}_R\right\}$ under the Restriction maps.
differentia: of Bloch--Deligne--Illusie
equipped with Restriction and Frobenius maps $R,F:W_r\Omega^n_R\to W_{r-1}\Omega^n_R$

nodes.name: Hesselholt's HKR theorem for $\TR$
nodes.statement: Let $R$ be a smooth $\mathbb{F}_p$-algebra. Then, for each $s\ge1$, we have an isomorphism of graded rings \begin{equation} \TR^s_*(R; p) \simeq W_s \Omega^{\ast}_R \otimes_{\mathbb{Z}/p^s} \mathbb{Z}/p^s [ \sigma_s], \quad |\sigma_s| = 2. \end{equation} The Restriction maps are determined by the Restriction maps on the de Rham--Witt complex and send $\sigma_s \mapsto p \sigma_{s-1}$. Therefore, we have an isomorphism \begin{equation} \TR_*(R; p) \simeq W \Omega^{\ast}_R, \end{equation} and the $F$ map on $\TR(R; p)$ induces the $F$ map on $W \Omega_R^{\ast}$.
nodes.statement_short: For smooth $\mathbb{F}_p$-algebras, $\TR^s_*$ is the de Rham--Witt complex tensored with a polynomial generator in degree 2.
assumptions: Let $R$ be a smooth $\mathbb{F}_p$-algebra.
for each $s\ge1$
conclusions: we have an isomorphism of graded rings \begin{equation} \TR^s_*(R; p) \simeq W_s \Omega^{\ast}_R \otimes_{\mathbb{Z}/p^s} \mathbb{Z}/p^s [ \sigma_s], \quad |\sigma_s| = 2. \end{equation}
Therefore, we have an isomorphism \begin{equation} \TR_*(R; p) \simeq W \Omega^{\ast}_R, \end{equation} and the $F$ map on $\TR(R; p)$ induces the $F$ map on $W \Omega_R^{\ast}$.

nodes.name: $\TC/p$ commutes with filtered colimits of $\mathbb{F}_p$-algebras
nodes.statement: The functor $\op{CAlg}_{/\bb F_p}\to\Sp$, $R\mapsto \TC(R)/p$ commutes with filtered colimits.
nodes.statement_short: De Rham--Witt proof of finitariness of $\TC/p$ in the $\mathbb{F}_p$-algebra case.
assumptions: The functor $\op{CAlg}_{/\bb F_p}\to\Sp$, $R\mapsto \TC(R)/p$
conclusions: commutes with filtered colimits

nodes.name: Proof via de Rham--Witt that $\TC/p$ is finitary on $\mathbb{F}_p$-algebras
nodes.statement: Let $R=\op{colim}_iR_i$ be a filtered colimit of $\bb F_p$-algebras. By functorially picking simplicial resolutions of all the terms by ind-smooth $\bb F_p$-algebras, and recalling that $\TC/p$ commutes with geometric realizations of rings, we reduce to the case in which all the $R_i$ (hence also $R$ itself) are ind-smooth over $\bb F_p$. Next we use Hesselholt's HKR theorem. Since each $\TR^s(-;p)$ commutes with filtered colimits (induction on (\ref{keyformulaclassical})), as does $W_s\Omega^n_{-}$, the formula \eqref{HHKR1} remains valid for ind-smooth $\bb F_p$-algebras. By taking the inverse limit over $s$, we deduce that $\pi_*(\TR(R;p)) \simeq W\Omega_R^*$ for any ind-smooth $\bb F_p$-algebra $R$, i.e., \eqref{HHKR2} is valid in the ind-smooth case as well. Note here that each $W\Omega_R^n$ is $p$-torsion-free, by a basic property of the de Rham--Witt complex for smooth $\mathbb{F}_p$-algebras \cite[Cor.~I.3.6]{illusie-derham-witt} which can easily be extended to the ind-smooth case as it derives from the stronger assertion that each Restriction map $W_s \Omega_R^{\ast} \to W_{s-1} \Omega_R^{\ast}$ annihilates every element $x \in W_s \Omega_R^{\ast}$ with $px = 0$. As a result, we also conclude that $\pi_* ( \TR(R; p)/p) \simeq W \Omega_R^{\ast}/p$. Taking fixed points for the Frobenius, we find that $\pi_n(\TC(R)/p)$ fits into an exact sequence \[W\Omega^{n+1}_R/p\xto{F-1}W\Omega^{n+1}_R/p\To \pi_n(\TC(R)/p)\To W\Omega^{n}_R/p\xto{F-1}W\Omega^{n}_R/p,\] and similarly for each $R_i$. To complete the proof it is enough to show, for each $n\ge0$, that the kernel and cokernel of $F-1:W\Omega^{n}_-/p\to W\Omega^{n}_-/p$ commutes with our filtered colimit $R=\op{colim}_iR_i$; we stress that $W\Omega^{n}_-/p$ does not commute with filtered colimits. For any ind-smooth $\bb F_p$-algebra $R$, consider the commutative diagram \begin{equation} \xymatrix{ W\Omega^{n}_R/p\ar[r]^{F-1}\ar[d] & W\Omega^{n}_R/p\ar[d]\\ \Omega^n_R\ar[r]_{C^{-1}-1}&\Omega^n_R/d\Omega^{n-1}_R }. \end{equation} Here $C^{-1}$ is the inverse Cartier operator. To complete the proof we will show that the two horizontal arrows have isomorphic kernels (resp.\ cokernels), i.e., the square is both cartesian and cocartesian. To see this, it suffices to show that the map induced between the kernels of the vertical maps (which are surjective) is an isomorphism. The kernel of the map $W \Omega^n_R \to \Omega^n_R$ is generated by the images of $V, dV$ by \cite[Proposition I.3.18]{illusie-derham-witt}. Note that the citation is for smooth $\mathbb{F}_p$-algebras, but the statement clearly passes to an ind-smooth algebra as the terms $W_s \Omega^n_{-}$ commute with filtered colimits and $W \Omega^n_{-} = \varprojlim W_s \Omega^n_{-}$. It follows that the kernel of the first vertical map in \eqref{thisdiag} is spanned by the images of $V, dV$ while the kernel of the second vertical map is spanned by the images of $V, d$. Thus, we need to show that the map \begin{equation} F - 1: \mathrm{im}\left(W \Omega^n_{R}/p\oplus W \Omega^{n-1}_{R}/p\xto{V+dV} W \Omega^n_{R}/p\right) \to \mathrm{im}\left(W \Omega^n_{R}/p\oplus W \Omega^{n-1}_{R}/p \xto{V+d} W \Omega^n_{R}/p\right) \end{equation} is an isomorphism. First, we show that $F-1$ is surjective. We record the following identities in $W \Omega_R^n/p$, \[(F-1)V=-V,\qquad (F-1)d\sum_{i>0}V^i=d;\] using it, we see immediately that $F - 1$ is surjective in \eqref{mapFminusone}. To see injectivity, we will use an important property of the de Rham--Witt complex: the image of $F$ on $W \Omega_R^n$ consists precisely of those elements $w$ with $dw$ divisible by $p$, thanks to \cite[(I.3.21.1.5)]{illusie-derham-witt}. Again, the reference is stated in the smooth case, but it also passes to the ind-smooth case;\footnote{Since the passage to the ind-smooth case is not completely immediate, we provide the argument. Firstly, the quasi-isomorphisms $W_s \Omega_R^\bullet/p\simeq \Omega_R^{\bullet}$ for $s\ge1$ in the smooth case \cite[Corol.~I.3.15]{illusie-derham-witt} extend at once to the ind-smooth case, and taking the limit then shows $W \Omega_R^\bullet/p\simeq \Omega_R^\bullet$ (to take the limit recall again that the $p$-torsion in $W_s\Omega^n_R$ is annihilated by $R:W_s\Omega^n_R\to W_{s-1}\Omega^n_R$). Secondly, the identity $\ker(d \colon \Omega^n_R\to\Omega^{n+1}_R)=\mathrm{Im}( F \colon W_2\Omega^n_R\to \Omega^n_R)$ also extends at once from the smooth \cite[Prop.~I.3.21]{illusie-derham-witt} to the ind-smooth case. Therefore, given $w\in W\Omega^n_R$ satisfying $dw\in pW\Omega^n_R$, we may write $w=Fx+y$ for some $x,y\in W\Omega^n_R$ such that $y$ vanishes in $\Omega^n_R$. But then $dy=dw-pFdx\in pW\Omega^n_R$, so $y$ defines a class in $H^n(W\Omega^\bullet/p)$ which vanishes in $H^n(\Omega^\bullet_R)$; by the first claim, we deduce that the initial class was zero, in other words that $y=dz+pz'$ for some $z\in W\Omega^{n-1}_R$, $z'\in W\Omega^n_R$. So $w= Fx+FdVz+FVz'$, as required.} for more on this point cf.~\cite[Sec.~2]{BLM}. Suppose $x \in W \Omega^n_R$ can be written as $x = Vy + dVz$ and $(F -1 )x $ is divisible by $p$; we show that $x $ is divisible by $p$ in $ W \Omega^n_R$. This will hold if $y, z \in \mathrm{im}(F)$. First, $-dx \equiv d((F-1) x)$ modulo $p$, so $dx$ is divisible by $p$. It follows that $d Vy$, and hence $dy = FdVy$ is divisible by $p$, so that $y$ belongs to the image of $F$. In particular, modulo $p$, we have $x \equiv dV z$ and $(F-1) d Vz = d (z - Vz)$ is divisible by $p$. Therefore, $z - Vz$ belongs to the image of $F$. Since the operator $V$ is topologically nilpotent on $W \Omega^n_R$, we find that $(1 - V)$ is invertible and $z \in \mathrm{im}(F)$. Therefore, $x$ is divisible by $p$ as desired.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to ind-smooth algebras, use Hesselholt's HKR to replace $\TC/p$ by $F-1$ on $W\Omega^n/p$, then show the comparison square with $C^{-1}-1$ is bicartesian.

nodes.name: Reduce to ind-smooth $\mathbb{F}_p$-algebras
nodes.statement: Let $R=\op{colim}_iR_i$ be a filtered colimit of $\bb F_p$-algebras. By functorially picking simplicial resolutions of all the terms by ind-smooth $\bb F_p$-algebras, and recalling that $\TC/p$ commutes with geometric realizations of rings, we reduce to the case in which all the $R_i$ (hence also $R$ itself) are ind-smooth over $\bb F_p$.
nodes.statement_short: Resolve by ind-smooth algebras to reduce to the ind-smooth case.

nodes.name: Compute $\pi_*(\TR(R;p)/p)$ via HKR and $p$-torsion-freeness
nodes.statement: Next we use Hesselholt's HKR theorem. Since each $\TR^s(-;p)$ commutes with filtered colimits (induction on (\ref{keyformulaclassical})), as does $W_s\Omega^n_{-}$, the formula \eqref{HHKR1} remains valid for ind-smooth $\bb F_p$-algebras. By taking the inverse limit over $s$, we deduce that $\pi_*(\TR(R;p)) \simeq W\Omega_R^*$ for any ind-smooth $\bb F_p$-algebra $R$, i.e., \eqref{HHKR2} is valid in the ind-smooth case as well. Note here that each $W\Omega_R^n$ is $p$-torsion-free, by a basic property of the de Rham--Witt complex for smooth $\mathbb{F}_p$-algebras \cite[Cor.~I.3.6]{illusie-derham-witt} which can easily be extended to the ind-smooth case as it derives from the stronger assertion that each Restriction map $W_s \Omega_R^{\ast} \to W_{s-1} \Omega_R^{\ast}$ annihilates every element $x \in W_s \Omega_R^{\ast}$ with $px = 0$. As a result, we also conclude that $\pi_* ( \TR(R; p)/p) \simeq W \Omega_R^{\ast}/p$.
nodes.statement_short: Extend Hesselholt's HKR isomorphism to ind-smooth algebras and reduce mod $p$.

nodes.name: Reduce to kernels and cokernels of $F-1$ on $W\Omega^n/p$
nodes.statement: Taking fixed points for the Frobenius, we find that $\pi_n(\TC(R)/p)$ fits into an exact sequence \[W\Omega^{n+1}_R/p\xto{F-1}W\Omega^{n+1}_R/p\To \pi_n(\TC(R)/p)\To W\Omega^{n}_R/p\xto{F-1}W\Omega^{n}_R/p,\] and similarly for each $R_i$. To complete the proof it is enough to show, for each $n\ge0$, that the kernel and cokernel of $F-1:W\Omega^{n}_-/p\to W\Omega^{n}_-/p$ commutes with our filtered colimit $R=\op{colim}_iR_i$; we stress that $W\Omega^{n}_-/p$ does not commute with filtered colimits.
nodes.statement_short: Rewrite the goal as commutation of $\ker$ and $\coker$ of $F-1$ with filtered colimits.

nodes.name: Compare with $C^{-1}-1$ on $\Omega^n_R$ via a bicartesian square
nodes.statement: For any ind-smooth $\bb F_p$-algebra $R$, consider the commutative diagram \begin{equation} \xymatrix{ W\Omega^{n}_R/p\ar[r]^{F-1}\ar[d] & W\Omega^{n}_R/p\ar[d]\\ \Omega^n_R\ar[r]_{C^{-1}-1}&\Omega^n_R/d\Omega^{n-1}_R }. \end{equation} Here $C^{-1}$ is the inverse Cartier operator. To complete the proof we will show that the two horizontal arrows have isomorphic kernels (resp.\ cokernels), i.e., the square is both cartesian and cocartesian.
nodes.statement_short: Introduce the comparison square with the inverse Cartier operator.

nodes.name: Surjectivity of $F-1$ on the relevant images
nodes.statement: First, we show that $F-1$ is surjective. We record the following identities in $W \Omega_R^n/p$, \[(F-1)V=-V,\qquad (F-1)d\sum_{i>0}V^i=d;\] using it, we see immediately that $F - 1$ is surjective in \eqref{mapFminusone}.
nodes.statement_short: Use the identities $(F-1)V=-V$ and $(F-1)d\sum V^i = d$ to get surjectivity.

nodes.name: Injectivity of $F-1$ using the image of $F$
nodes.statement: Suppose $x \in W \Omega^n_R$ can be written as $x = Vy + dVz$ and $(F -1 )x $ is divisible by $p$; we show that $x $ is divisible by $p$ in $ W \Omega^n_R$. This will hold if $y, z \in \mathrm{im}(F)$. First, $-dx \equiv d((F-1) x)$ modulo $p$, so $dx$ is divisible by $p$. It follows that $d Vy$, and hence $dy = FdVy$ is divisible by $p$, so that $y$ belongs to the image of $F$. In particular, modulo $p$, we have $x \equiv dV z$ and $(F-1) d Vz = d (z - Vz)$ is divisible by $p$. Therefore, $z - Vz$ belongs to the image of $F$. Since the operator $V$ is topologically nilpotent on $W \Omega^n_R$, we find that $(1 - V)$ is invertible and $z \in \mathrm{im}(F)$. Therefore, $x$ is divisible by $p$ as desired.
nodes.statement_short: Show $y,z \in \mathrm{im}(F)$ using divisibility of $dx$ and topological nilpotence of $V$.

nodes.name: saturated Dieudonn\'e complex
nodes.statement: A \emph{saturated} Dieudonn\'e complex $(X^{\ast}, d, F)$ is a $p$-torsion-free cochain complex equipped with an operator $F: X^{\ast} \to X^{\ast}$ such that $dF = pFd$, the opeartor $F: X^n \to X^n$ is injective, and the image of $F$ consists precisely of those $x \in X^n$ such that $p $ divides $dx$; this implies that one can define uniquely an operator $V$ such that $FV = VF = p$.
differentia: equipped with an operator $F: X^{\ast} \to X^{\ast}$ such that $dF = pFd$
the opeartor $F: X^n \to X^n$ is injective
the image of $F$ consists precisely of those $x \in X^n$ such that $p $ divides $dx$

nodes.name: strict Dieudonn\'e complex
nodes.statement: A saturated Dieudonn\'e complex $(X^{\ast}, d, F)$ is called \emph{strict} if $X^{\ast}$ is in addition complete for the filtration defined by $\{\mathrm{im}(V^n, d V^n)\}$.
differentia: $X^{\ast}$ is in addition complete for the filtration defined by $\{\mathrm{im}(V^n, d V^n)\}$

nodes.name: Kernel and cokernel of $F-1$ on strict Dieudonn\'e complexes are finitary
nodes.statement: The functors from the category of strict Dieudonn\'e complexes to graded abelian groups given by $$(X^{\ast}, d, F)\mapsto \mathrm{ker}(F-1: X^{\ast}/p \to X^{\ast}/p), \quad \mathrm{coker}( F-1 : X^{\ast}/p \to X^{\ast}/p) $$ commute with filtered colimits.
nodes.statement_short: $\ker$ and $\coker$ of $F-1$ mod $p$ commute with filtered colimits of strict Dieudonn\'e complexes.
assumptions: The functors from the category of strict Dieudonn\'e complexes to graded abelian groups given by $(X^{\ast}, d, F)\mapsto \mathrm{ker}(F-1: X^{\ast}/p \to X^{\ast}/p), \quad \mathrm{coker}( F-1 : X^{\ast}/p \to X^{\ast}/p)$
conclusions: commute with filtered colimits

nodes.name: nonunital $R$-algebra
nodes.statement: Given a commutative base ring $R$, a \emph{nonunital $R$-algebra} is an $R$-module $I$ equipped with a multiplication map $I \otimes_R I \to I$ which is commutative and associative. We denote the category of nonunital $R$-algebras by $\nur$. By contrast, when we say ``$R$-algebra,'' we assume the existence of a unit.
differentia: equipped with a multiplication map $I \otimes_R I \to I$ which is commutative and associative

nodes.name: Free nonunital $R$-algebra on $n$ generators
nodes.statement: Let $R[x_1, \dots, x_n]^+$ denote the ideal $(x_1, \dots, x_n) \subset R[x_1, \dots, x_n]$ in the polynomial ring $R[x_1, \dots, x_n]$. Then $R[x_1, \dots, x_n]^+$ is the free object of $\nur$ on $n$ generators.

nodes.name: short exact sequence in $\nur$
nodes.statement: We say that a sequence $I' \to I \to \overline{I}$ in $\nur$ is a \emph{short exact sequence} if it is a short exact sequence of underlying abelian groups. That is, $I \to \overline{I}$ is surjective, and we can recover $I'$ as the pullback $0 \times_{\overline{I}} I$ in the category $\nur$.
differentia: it is a short exact sequence of underlying abelian groups

nodes.name: local nonunital $R$-algebra
nodes.statement: A non-unital $R$-algebra $I$ is \emph{local} if the following equivalent conditions hold: \begin{enumerate} \item For any $x \in I$, there exists $y \in I$ (necessarily unique) such that $x + y + xy = 0$. \item Whenever $I$ embeds as an ideal in an $R$-algebra $S$, then $I$ is contained in the Jacobson radical of $S$. \item $I \subset R \ltimes I$ is contained in the Jacobson radical of $R \ltimes I$. \end{enumerate} The equivalence of the above conditions follows because, given an ideal $I \subset S$ in a commutative ring $S$, then $I$ belongs to the Jacobson radical of $S$ if and only if $1 + I$ consists of units of $S$. We let $\nuloc \subset \nur$ denote the full subcategory of nonunital local $R$-algebras.
nodes.statement_short: A nonunital algebra is local iff every element has a quasi-inverse, equivalently iff it lies in the Jacobson radical of any unitalization.
differentia: For any $x \in I$, there exists $y \in I$ (necessarily unique) such that $x + y + xy = 0$

nodes.name: Construction of the localization $I[(1+I)^{-1}]$
nodes.statement: \begin{equation} I[(1+I)^{-1}] := I\otimes_{R[1+I]} R[(1+I)^{gp}], \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Formula for the left adjoint to $\nuloc \subset \nur$.

nodes.name: Free local nonunital $R$-algebra $R[x_1,\dots,x_n]^+_{(x_1,\dots,x_n)}$
nodes.statement: Let $R[x_1, \dots, x_n]^+_{(x_1, \dots, x_n)}\in\nuloc$ be the image of $R[x_1, \dots, x_n]^+\in\nur$ under the left adjoint explained above. In other words, $R[x_1, \dots, x_n]^+_{(x_1, \dots, x_n)}$ is the ideal $(x_1, \dots, x_n)$ of the localization $R[x_1, \dots, x_n]_{1 + (x_1, \dots, x_n)}$ of the polynomial ring $R[x_1, \dots, x_n]$ at its multiplicative subset $1 + (x_1, \dots, x_n)$. It follows that $R[x_1, \dots, x_n]^+_{(x_1, \dots, x_n)}$ is a local nonunital $R$-algebra, and it is the free object on $n$ generators.

nodes.name: $\nuloc \subset \nur$ as a localization, independent of the base ring
nodes.statement:
Stated more formally, the preceding discussion shows that the inclusion $
uloc \subset 
ur$ is the right adjoint of a \emph{localization} functor on the category $
ur$. Specifically, $
uloc$ consists of those objects in $I \in 
ur$ which are orthogonal \cite[Sec. 5.4]{Borceux1} to the map $R[x]^+ 	o R[x]^+_{1 + (x)}$, in the sense that such that any map $R[x]^+ 	o I$ extends uniquely over $R[x]^+_{1 + (x)}$. Moreover, one sees easily from the construction of the localization \eqref{loccons} that it is independent of the ground ring $R$. Analogous statements will be true when we restrict further to the subcategory of henselian nonunital rings; see the proof of Lemma ef{lemma_nuh}.
nodes.statement_short: $\nuloc$ is the orthogonal of $R[x]^+ \to R[x]^+_{1+(x)}$, and the localization does not depend on $R$.

nodes.name: henselian nonunital $R$-algebra
nodes.statement: A nonunital $R$-algebra $I$ is \emph{henselian} if for every $n \geq 1$ and every polynomial $g(x) \in I[x]$, the equation \begin{equation} x(1 + x)^{n-1} + g(x) = 0 \end{equation} has a solution in $I$. We let $\nuh \subset \nur$ denote the full subcategory of henselian nonunital $R$-algebras.
differentia: for every $n \geq 1$ and every polynomial $g(x) \in I[x]$, the equation $x(1 + x)^{n-1} + g(x) = 0$ has a solution in $I$

nodes.name: The henselian equation $x(1+x)^{n-1} + g(x) = 0$
nodes.statement: \begin{equation} x(1 + x)^{n-1} + g(x) = 0 \end{equation}

nodes.name: Henselian nonunital algebras are local, with unique roots
nodes.statement: We note that if $I$ is a henselian nonunital $R$-algebra then: \begin{enumerate} \item Considering the equation $x + xy + y = 0$ for $y \in I$, we find that $I$ is local, i.e., $\nuh \subset \nuloc$. \item The root of the equation \eqref{henseq} is necessarily unique: denoting the equation by $f(x)=0$ for simplicity, if $\alpha, \alpha' \in I$ are both roots then we have $f'(\alpha) \in 1 + I$ and so the Taylor expansion shows that $$0 = f(\alpha) - f(\alpha') \in \alpha - \alpha' + I(\alpha - \alpha'),$$ whence $\alpha = \alpha'$ since $I$ is local. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: $\nuh \subset \nuloc$, and the root of the henselian equation is unique.

nodes.name: $\nuh$ is presentable and admits a left adjoint (henselization)
nodes.statement:
The category $
uh$ is presentable and the inclusion $
uh \subset 
ur$ admits a left adjoint.
nodes.statement_short: Existence of the henselization left adjoint $\nur \to \nuh$.
assumptions: The category $\nuh$
conclusions: is presentable and the inclusion $\nuh \subset \nur$ admits a left adjoint

nodes.name: Proof that $\nuh$ is presentable with a left adjoint
nodes.statement:
It follows from the above discussion that $
uh$ is the orthogonal \cite[Sec.~5.4]{Borceux1} of $
ur$ with respect to the maps \[ f_{n,t}: R[x_0, \dots, x_t]^+ 	o R[x_0, \dots, x_t, y]^+/( y(1 + y)^{n-1} + x_0 + x_1 y + \dots + x_t y^t ),\] for $n, t \geq 1$. That is, a given object $X \in 
ur$ belongs to $
uh$ if and only  egin{equation} \hom_{
ur}( R[x_0, \dots, x_t, y]^+/( y(1 + y)^{n-1} + x_0 + x_1 y + \dots + x_t y^t ), X) \xto{\cdot\circ f_{n,t}} \hom_{
ur}(R[x_0, \dots, x_t]^+ , X) \end{equation} is an isomorphism for all $n,t\ge1$. It now follows formally that $
uh$ is presentable and the desired left adjoint exists \cite[Cor. 5.4.8]{Borceux1}. Alternatively, one can appeal to the theory of henselian pairs and define the left adjoint directly by taking the henselization of the pair $(R \ltimes I, I)$; see the forthcoming Construction ef{construction_henselization}.
nodes.statement_short: Exhibit $\nuh$ as an orthogonality class and quote the general adjoint-functor theorem.

nodes.name: Free henselian nonunital algebra $R\{x_1,\dots,x_n\}^+$
nodes.statement:
Let $R\left\{x_1, \dots, x_night\}^+\in 
uh$ denote the henselization of $R[x_1, \dots, x_n]^+ \in 
ur$. By construction, $R\left\{x_1, \dots, x_night\}^+ \in 
uh$ is the free object on $n$ generators.

nodes.name:
$
ur$, $
uloc$, $
uh$ as models of a Lawvere theory
nodes.statement:
The categories $
ur$, $
uloc$ and $
uh$ are all examples of models for a {\em Lawvere} or {\em algebraic theory} \cite[Ch.~3]{ARloc} \cite[Ch.~3]{Borceux}. Let $\mathcal{C}$ be a category satisfying the following conditions:  egin{itemize} \item[(Law)] $\mathcal C$ has all limits and colimits, and is equipped with a functor $U \colon \mathcal C	o \mathrm{Sets}$ which is conservative, preserves sifted colimits, and admits a left adjoint $F \colon \mathrm{Sets}	o\mathcal C$. \end{itemize} For example, $\mathcal C$ might be the category of rings, nonunital rings, groups, etc. In this case, one takes for $U$ the forgetful functor taking the underlying set, and its right adjoint $F$ is the free ring, nonunital ring, group, etc.~on the given set. Denoting by $\{1\}$ a one-point set, the element $F(\{1\})$ is therefore both compact projective (i.e., $\hom_{\mathcal{C}}(F(\{1\}), \cdot)$ commutes with sifted colimits) and a strong generator (i.e., $\hom_{\mathcal{C}}(F(\{1\}), \cdot)$ is faithful and conservative). The {\em free object of $\mathcal C$ on $n$ generators} is by definition $ igsqcup_nF(\{1\})\simeq F(\{1,\dots,n\})$. By the monadicity theorem, $\mathcal{C}$ is monadic over $\mathrm{Sets}$, via a monad that preserves sifted colimits. Let $\mathcal C'\subset \mathcal C$ be a full subcategory, and assume that $\mathcal C'$ is closed under limits and sifted colimits (in $\mathcal C$) and that the inclusion $\mathcal C'\subset\mathcal C$ is a right adjoint. Then clearly $\mathcal C'$ also satisfies conditions (Law), with $U'$ given by the restriction of $U$ to $\mathcal C'$. Moreover, the free objects of $\mathcal C'$ are given by applying the left adjoint $\mathcal C	o \mathcal C'$ to the free objects of $\mathcal C$. In practice, this is how the ``free objects'' in the above categories are constructed. According to general results of Lawvere theory \cite[Thm.~3.9.1]{Borceux} (in fact, we do not use the results in this paragraph, but the point of view may be helpful), the full subcategory $\mathcal{C}_{\Sigma} \subset \mathcal{C}$ of compact projective objects of $\mathcal{C}$ is the idempotent completion of the full subcategory consisting of the free objects $\left\{ igsqcup_{n} F(\{1\}) : n \geq 0ight\}$. Furthermore, $\mathcal{C}$ can be identified with the category of presheaves on $\mathcal{C}_\Sigma$ which commute with finite products. In particular, objects of $\mathcal{C}$ can be identified with sets equipped with various ``operations'' arising from maps between the free objects satisfying various relations.
nodes.statement_short: Formalizes condition (Law) and identifies the compact projective objects with the idempotent completion of the free objects.

nodes.name: pair, henselian pair, henselian local ring
nodes.statement: A \emph{pair} is the data $(S, I)$ where $S$ is a commutative ring and $I \subset S$ is an ideal. The collection of pairs forms a category in the obvious manner. The pair $(S, I)$ is said to be \emph{henselian} if the following equivalent (cf.~\cite[Tag 09XD]{stacks-project} for the equivalence) conditions hold: \begin{enumerate} \item Given a polynomial $f(x) \in S[x]$ and a root $\overline{\alpha} \in S/I$ of $\overline{f} \in (S/I)[x]$ with $\overline{f}'(\alpha)$ being a unit of $S/I$, then $\overline \alpha$ lifts to a root $\alpha \in S$ of $f$. Note that the lifted root $\alpha \in S$ is necessarily unique by the same argument as we gave after Definition \ref{def_hens_nu}. \item The ideal $I$ is contained in the Jacobson radical of $S$, and the same condition as (1) holds for \emph{monic} polynomials $f(x) \in S[x]$. \item Given any commutative diagram \begin{equation} \xymatrix{ A \ar[d] \ar[r] & S \ar[d] \\ B \ar[r] \ar@{-->}[ru] & S/I\ }\end{equation} with $A \to B$ \'etale, there exists a lift as in the dotted arrow. \end{enumerate} We may also say that the surjective map $S \to S/I$ is a henselian pair, if there is no risk of confusion. If $S$ is local with maximal ideal $\frak m$, then $S$ is said to be a \emph{henselian local ring} if $(S, \frak m)$ is a henselian pair.
nodes.origin_citation: Stacks Project Tag 09XD; Raynaud, Ch. XI
nodes.statement_short: Three equivalent characterizations of a henselian pair, including the \'etale right-lifting property.
differentia: Given a polynomial $f(x) \in S[x]$ and a root $\overline{\alpha} \in S/I$ of $\overline{f} \in (S/I)[x]$ with $\overline{f}'(\alpha)$ being a unit of $S/I$, then $\overline \alpha$ lifts to a root $\alpha \in S$ of $f$

Given any commutative diagram \begin{equation} \xymatrix{ A \ar[d] \ar[r] & S \ar[d] \\ B \ar[r] \ar@{-->}[ru] & S/I\ }\end{equation} with $A \to B$ \'etale, there exists a lift as in the dotted arrow

nodes.name: Uniqueness in the lifting property
nodes.statement: Let $(S, I)$ be a henselian pair and consider a diagram as in \eqref{lifthens} with $A \to B$ \'etale. Then the lifting is unique. Indeed, given two liftings $f_1, f_2: B \to S$ in \eqref{lifthens}, we have a commutative diagram \[ \xymatrix{ B \otimes_A B \ar[d]^m \ar[r]^{f_1 \otimes f_2} & S \ar[d] \\ B \ar[r] & S/I, }\] for $m \colon B \otimes_A B \to B$ the multiplication map. Since $m$ is also \'etale (in fact, the projection on a direct factor), the lifting property again shows that $f_1 \otimes f_2$ factors through $m$, so $f_1 = f_2$.
nodes.statement_short: \'Etale lifts along a henselian pair are unique, by applying the lifting property to $B \otimes_A B \to B$.

nodes.name: Subideals of a henselian ideal remain henselian
nodes.statement: Let $(R, I)$ be a henselian pair and let $J \subset I$ be a subideal. Then $(R, J)$ remains a henselian pair.

nodes.name: Elkik's theorem (smooth lifting along a henselian pair)
nodes.statement: Let $(S, I)$ be a henselian pair. Then $S \to S/I$ has the right lifting property with respect to smooth maps. That is, any diagram as in \eqref{lifthens} with $A \to B$ smooth (rather than \'etale) admits a lift as in the dotted arrow.
nodes.statement_short: Henselian pairs have the right lifting property against smooth maps, not just \'etale ones.
assumptions: Let $(S, I)$ be a henselian pair.
conclusions: Then $S \to S/I$ has the right lifting property with respect to smooth maps.

nodes.name: Henselianness of a pair depends only on the nonunital ring $I$
nodes.statement: Let $(S, I)$ be a pair. Then $(S, I)$ is a henselian pair if and only if $I$ is henselian as a nonunital ring.
nodes.origin_citation: Gabber [gabber], Prop. 1; cf. Raynaud Prop. XI.1
nodes.statement_short: Gabber's observation: henselianness of $(S,I)$ only depends on $I$ as a nonunital ring.
assumptions: Let $(S, I)$ be a pair.
conclusions: Then $(S, I)$ is a henselian pair if and only if $I$ is henselian as a nonunital ring.

nodes.name: Henselianness is detected by $(\mathbb{Z} \ltimes I, I)$
nodes.statement: Let $(S, I)$ be a pair. Then $(S, I)$ is a henselian pair if and only if $(\mathbb{Z} \ltimes I, I)$ is a henselian pair.
assumptions: Let $(S, I)$ be a pair.
conclusions: Then $(S, I)$ is a henselian pair if and only if $(\mathbb{Z} \ltimes I, I)$ is a henselian pair.

nodes.name: Construction of the henselization of a pair
nodes.statement: Given a pair $(S, I)$, there is a pair $(S^h, I^h)$ and a map $(S, I) \to (S^h, I^h)$, called the \emph{henselization} of the original pair, with the following properties. \begin{enumerate} \item $(S^h, I^h)$ is a henselian pair and is the initial henselian pair receiving a map from $(S, I)$. That is, the construction $(S, I) \mapsto (S^h, I^h)$ is the left adjoint to the forgetful functor from henselian pairs to pairs. \item $S^h$ is a filtered colimit of \'etale $S$-algebras and $I^h = I S^h = I \otimes_S S^h$. \item The map $S/I \to S^h/I^h$ is an isomorphism. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Every pair admits a henselization, universal among henselian pairs, ind-\'etale over $S$ and with the same quotient.
assumptions: Given a pair $(S, I)$
conclusions: there is a pair $(S^h, I^h)$ and a map $(S, I) \to (S^h, I^h)$, called the \emph{henselization} of the original pair
$(S^h, I^h)$ is a henselian pair and is the initial henselian pair receiving a map from $(S, I)$
$S^h$ is a filtered colimit of \'etale $S$-algebras and $I^h = I S^h = I \otimes_S S^h$
The map $S/I \to S^h/I^h$ is an isomorphism.

nodes.name: Recognizing the henselization via ind-\'etale factorizations
nodes.statement: Let $(S, I)$ be a pair. Suppose given a factorization $S \to \widetilde{S} \to S/I$ such that $\widetilde{S}$ is a filtered colimit of \'etale $S$-algebras and such that $\widetilde{S} \to S/I$ has the right lifting property with respect to \'etale morphisms (i.e., the surjection $\widetilde{S} \to S/I$ is a henselian pair). Then $(\widetilde{S}, I \widetilde{S})$ is the henselization of $(S, I)$. To see this, consider a henselian pair $(A, J)$ and a map $(S, I) \to (A, J)$. Considering the commutative diagram \[ \xymatrix{ S \ar[d] \ar[r] & \widetilde{S} \ar@{-->}[ld] \ar[r] & S/I \ar[d] \\ A \ar[rr] & & A/J },\] the ind-\'etaleness of $S \to \widetilde{S}$ implies the existence of a \emph{unique} dotted arrow $\widetilde{S} \to A$ making the diagram commute (cf.~Remark~\ref{uniquenessinliftingproperty}). This verifies the universal property of the henselization. In particular, one can construct $(S^h, I^h)$ by appealing to Quillen's small object argument \cite[Th. 2.1.14]{Hovey} to factor $S \to S/I$ as the composite of a filtered colimit of \'etale morphisms and a morphism that has the right lifting property with respect to \'etale morphisms; the universal property of the henselization then constructs it as a functor. Note that in \eqref{lifthens}, it suffices to take $A, B$ finitely generated over $\mathbb{Z}$, by the structure theory for \'etale morphisms.
nodes.statement_short: An ind-\'etale factorization with the \'etale right lifting property computes the henselization; Quillen's small object argument constructs it.

nodes.name: Milnor square
nodes.statement: A \emph{Milnor square} of commutative rings is a diagram \begin{equation} \xymatrix{ S \ar[d] \ar[r]& T \ar[d] \\ S' \ar[r] & T' } \end{equation} such that the vertical arrows are surjective and such that the diagram is both cartesian and cocartesian in the category of commutative rings. It follows in particular that if $I \subset S$, $J \subset T$ are the respective kernels of the vertical maps $S \to S'$, $T \to T'$, then $f|_I : I \isoto J$ establishes an isomorphism of the ideals $I$, $J$.
differentia: the vertical arrows are surjective
the diagram is both cartesian and cocartesian in the category of commutative rings

nodes.name: Henselization of a Milnor square is a Milnor square
nodes.statement: Consider a Milnor square as in \eqref{milnsquare} with respect to the ideals $I \subset S$, $J \subset T$.
